subtopic: Recovering from a major work mistake
subtype: Approach: sharing lessons with the wider team [Revision]
passage:
At the milk collection centre on the edge of town, Deepika had typed the wrong fat readings for a whole morning, and eleven farmers were paid less than they should have been. She caught it the next day, put it right and paid the difference. Her hands still shook.
On Friday she stood before the team of six for ten minutes. "This is what went wrong. I copied the numbers from a smudged slip. This is what changed: I now read each figure back aloud to one other person."
The room was quiet. Then Kalyani said, "I nearly did the same last week and told no one."
Within a month there was a paper on the wall called "Near Misses", and four names had already written on it.

qa.q: How many farmers were paid less than they should have been?
What was Deepika feeling before giving the talk?
qa.a: Deepika was nervous and ashamed, with hands that still shook after the mistake.

qa.q: What could Deepika do to keep the near-miss paper useful?
qa.a: Deepika could read the entries at each Friday meeting and note which changes were made from them.

qa.q: How might Kalyani have felt admitting a near miss aloud?
qa.a: Kalyani probably felt relieved and a little brave, since Deepika's openness made it safe to admit it.

grounding: The passage shows an employee giving a short talk on what failed and what changed, after which others start reporting near misses, making the team safer.

subtopic: Recovering from a major work mistake
subtype: Approach: sharing lessons with the wider team [Revision]
passage:
In the Johannesburg office, on a grey Thursday afternoon, Jamal stood in front of thirty colleagues with five slides. Two months earlier, his change had pushed a wrong exchange rate into the pricing system for three hours.
'Here's what failed,' he said. 'I skipped the second review because the release was late. The alert went to an inbox nobody watched. And the rollback took forty minutes because nobody had ever tried it.' Next slide. 'Here's what changed: no skipping review, alerts go to the on-call phone, rollback is tested monthly.'
Nobody laughed or whispered. The next week, Zanele from the data team posted in the shared channel: 'Near miss. I almost ran a delete on the wrong table. Here's what stopped me.' Two more posts like it followed that month.

qa.q: How long was the wrong exchange rate in the pricing system?
What might Jamal have been feeling in front of thirty colleagues?
qa.a: He was probably nervous and exposed, though his clear slides suggest he felt ready to own it.

qa.q: What else could the team do to keep near-miss reporting going?
qa.a: Leaders could thank people for each near-miss post and share the fixes, so reporting keeps feeling safe.

qa.q: How might Zanele have been affected by Jamal's talk?
qa.a: Seeing Jamal speak openly without ridicule likely made Zanele feel safe enough to post a near miss too.

grounding: It shows an employee presenting what failed and what changed, after which others start reporting near misses and the team becomes safer.

subtopic: Recovering from a major work mistake
subtype: Approach: sharing lessons with the wider team [Revision]
passage:
The monthly lunch-and-learn in the bank's operations centre was usually about new software. This time Nandini stood by the projector with a slide that read: 'How I sent 600 duplicate SMS alerts.'
People sat up. She walked through it: a retry setting she had copied from an old project, a test that only checked one message, a Friday release with no second pair of eyes. Then the fixes: a review for any change to notifications, a test that counts messages, no Friday releases for customer alerts.
'I'm telling you because it was easy to do,' she said. 'Any of us could.'
Three days later, Devika from the cards team emailed her: 'Almost did the same with a card-block message. Your slide made me check the count. Can I add my near miss to your list?' Nandini started a shared page that afternoon.

qa.q: What did Nandini's first slide read?
What made Devika email Nandini, and how did Devika probably feel?
qa.a: Devika likely felt a jolt of alarm at nearly repeating the mistake, then relief and gratitude that the slide made her check the count.

qa.q: What else could Nandini do with the shared page?
qa.a: She could go through it at each lunch-and-learn and turn repeated near misses into new checks, so lessons spread across teams.

qa.q: How might the audience see Nandini's openness?
qa.a: They may be surprised at first, then more willing to admit their own slips, since she showed it was easy to do.

grounding: It shows an employee giving a short talk on what failed and what changed, and others starting to report near misses.
